title: People & Family
description: The people around you: family, partners, friends and guests. Family comes up early in Indonesian small talk, so you'll use these straight away.

items.registerNotes: Also for nationality: orang Indonesia (an Indonesian), orang Selandia Baru (a New Zealander). After a number it counts people: dua orang, two people.
Signs and forms use the more formal pria (look for it on toilet doors); friends say cowok. Anak laki-laki is a son or a boy.
Signs and forms use the more formal wanita (look for it on toilet doors); friends say cewek. Anak perempuan is a daughter or a girl.
Anak saya is my child, whatever their age.
items.cultureNote: Sudah punya anak? (Do you have children yet?) is an ordinary question soon after meeting someone, not a nosy one.

items.registerNotes: Capitalised, Ibu (or Bu for short) is how you address any grown woman politely: Terima kasih, Bu. With a woman you don't know, use it instead of 'you': Ibu tinggal di sini? (Do you live here?)
Capitalised, Bapak (or Pak for short) is how you address any grown man politely: Permisi, Pak. With a man you don't know, use it instead of 'you': Bapak dari mana? (Where are you from?)
The usual word for talking about someone's father: ayah saya, my father. Bapak means father too, but you'll mostly hear it as a way of addressing men.

items.pitfallNote: There's no word that means just 'brother' or 'sister': kakak is older and adik younger, of either sex. Add laki-laki or perempuan only if it matters: kakak perempuan, older sister.
items.cultureNote: Shortened to Kak, it's a friendly, polite way to address a young adult, and shop and café staff often use it with customers.

items.registerNotes: Adik laki-laki is a younger brother, adik perempuan a younger sister. Shortened to Dik (often said Dek), it's how adults address a child or a much younger stranger.

items.cultureNote: Sudah menikah? (Are you married?) is an ordinary question in a first conversation. If you're not, the polite answer is Belum (not yet) rather than tidak.

items.registerNotes: Also someone you share something with: teman kerja (a colleague), teman sekolah (a schoolmate). In casual speech it's often temen.
One word for either, so pacar saya can be my boyfriend or my girlfriend. Sudah punya pacar? (Have you got a boyfriend/girlfriend?) is a common, often teasing question.

items.cultureNote: Family is a big part of small talk: expect questions about your parents, brothers and sisters, partner and children soon after meeting, and it's friendly to ask back.

items.registerNotes: Many families say oma and opa instead, from Dutch, and Javanese families often say eyang for either grandparent.

items.cultureNote: A guest is always offered a drink. Wait until your host says Silakan diminum (Please, have a drink), then have at least a sip.

items.registerNotes: Nama saya … is 'My name is …'. To ask politely: Namanya siapa? or, to a woman, Nama Ibu siapa?
items.pitfallNote: For a person's name the question word is siapa (who), not apa. Namanya apa? is how you ask what a thing is called.
items.cultureNote: Many Indonesians have only one name, with no family name.
